title: Distributed Systems
objectives: This course introduces the principles, architectures, and mechanisms of distributed systems. Students learn the core concepts of processes, communication, time, coordination, consistency, replication, and fault tolerance; identify and handle concurrency, partial failures, and distributed-system faults; compare client-server, peer-to-peer, cloud, edge, and other distributed architectures; and analyze system-design trade-offs involving scalability, dependability, transparency, openness, performance, and security. The course develops the ability to reason about and design distributed systems using both fundamental algorithms and real-world architectural patterns.
syllabus:
1. Introduction to Distributed Systems: Distributed vs. decentralized systems; resource sharing and fundamental challenges; core design goals: distribution transparency, openness, dependability, security, and scalability; classification of distributed systems: high-performance distributed computing, distributed information systems, and pervasive/IoT systems.
2. System Architectures and Middleware: Architectural styles: layered, service-oriented, publish-subscribe, and component-connector architectures; middleware organization and services; centralized architectures: client-server, multitier architectures, Network File System (NFS), and Web architectures; decentralized architectures: structured and unstructured peer-to-peer systems, distributed hash tables (DHTs), and BitTorrent; hybrid architectures: cloud computing, edge-cloud systems, and blockchain architectures.
3. Processes, Virtualization, and Code Migration: Processes and threads in distributed environments, context switching, and multithreaded servers; virtualization, virtual machines, containers, and their role in distributed systems; clients, servers, networked user interfaces, virtual desktop environments, server design, object servers, and server clusters; code migration: motivation, weak and strong mobility, and migration in heterogeneous systems.
4. Interprocess and Distributed Communication: Communication foundations: layered protocols, TCP/UDP, and middleware communication; Remote Procedure Call (RPC): client/server stubs, parameter passing, data representation, and RPC semantics; message-oriented communication: sockets, ZeroMQ communication patterns, MPI, message queues, and message-oriented middleware; multicast communication: application-level multicast, overlay trees, flooding, and gossip-based dissemination.
5. Naming and Clock Synchronization: Naming in distributed systems: names, identifiers, addresses, flat and structured naming, name resolution, distributed hash tables, and directory services; clock synchronization: physical clocks, clock drift, precision and accuracy, and clock synchronization algorithms; logical time and event ordering: Lamport clocks and vector timestamps.
6. Distributed Coordination and Agreement: Distributed mutual exclusion: centralized, permission-based, Ricart-Agrawala, token-based, and decentralized approaches; leader election: bully and ring algorithms and coordinator selection; gossip-based coordination: aggregation, peer sampling, and overlay construction.
7. Consistency and Replication: Replication as a reliability and scalability technique; conflicting operations and consistency trade-offs; data-centric consistency models: sequential, causal, and eventual consistency; client-centric consistency models (monotonic reads/writes, read-your-writes); replica placement, content replication, caching, update propagation, and consistency protocols.
8. Fault Tolerance and Consensus: Failure models, redundancy, process groups, and failure masking; consensus and process resilience under crash failures, replicated state machines, and consensus principles; arbitrary and Byzantine failures: Byzantine agreement, majority voting, and fault-tolerant process groups.
textbooks:
1. Maarten van Steen and Andrew S. Tanenbaum, Distributed Systems, 4th Edition, 2024.
2. George Coulouris, Jean Dollimore, Tim Kindberg, and Gordon Blair, Distributed Systems: Concepts and Design, 5th Edition, Addison-Wesley.
